127: Believe me, dear Wilhelm, I was not thinking of you when I spoke so harshly of people who advise resignation to an inevitable fate.
I did not think you capable of such a sentiment.
But in fact you are right.
I have only one objection to make.
In this world one is seldom reduced to a choice between two alternatives.
There are as many varieties of conduct and opinion as there are gradations of feature between an aquiline nose and a flat one.
128: So you will allow me to grant your whole argument, and still contrive a way out of your dilemma.
129: Your position, as I hear it, is this: "Either you have hopes of winning Charlotte, or you have none."
"In the first case, hold your course and press on to the fulfilment of your wishes."
"In the second, be a man and shake off a miserable passion that will drain you and destroy you."
My dear friend, that is well said, and easily said.
130: But would you require a wretched creature, whose life is slowly wasting under a lingering disease, to finish himself off at once with a dagger?
Does the very disorder that eats away his strength not also rob him of the courage to deliver himself?
131: You may answer me, if you like, with an analogy of your own: "Who would not rather have an arm amputated than risk his life through doubt and delay?"
But I do not know whether I am right, and we had better leave these comparisons alone.
132: There are moments, Wilhelm, when I could get up and shake it all off, and when, if I only knew where to go, I would fly from this place.
134: My diary, which I have neglected for some time, came before me today; and I am amazed to see how deliberately I have entangled myself, step by step.
To have seen my position so clearly, and yet to have acted so like a child!
Even now I see the outcome plainly, and still have no thought of acting with any more prudence.
136: If I were not a fool, I could live the happiest and most delightful life here.
So many agreeable circumstances, of the kind that make a worthy man happy, are seldom found together.
I feel it too keenly — it is the heart alone that makes our happiness.
To be taken into this most charming family; to be loved by the father as a son, by the children as a father, and by Charlotte!
And then the noble Albert, who never disturbs my happiness by the least show of ill humour, who receives me with the heartiest affection and loves me, after Charlotte, better than all the world!
Wilhelm, you would be delighted to hear us on our rambles, talking about Charlotte.
Nothing in the world could be more absurd than our connection, and yet the thought of it often moves me to tears.
137: He tells me sometimes about her excellent mother.
How, on her deathbed, she gave her house and her children into Charlotte's keeping, and gave Charlotte herself into his.
How, from that time, a new spirit took possession of her; how, in her care and anxiety for their welfare, she became a real mother to them.
How every moment of her time was given to some labour of love on their behalf — and yet her cheerfulness never deserted her.
I walk at his side, pick flowers along the way, arrange them carefully into a nosegay, then throw them into the first stream I pass and watch them float gently away.
I forget whether I told you that Albert is to stay here.
He has been given a government appointment with a very good salary, and I understand he stands high in favour at court.
I have met few people so punctual and methodical in business.
139: Albert is certainly the best fellow in the world.
I had a strange scene with him yesterday.
I went to take my leave of him, having taken it into my head to spend a few days in these mountains, from where I am writing to you now.
As I walked up and down his room, my eye fell on his pistols.
"Lend me those pistols," I said, "for my journey."
"By all means," he replied, "if you will take the trouble to load them; they only hang there for form."
I took one of them down, and he went on: "Ever since I came near suffering for my own excessive caution, I will have nothing to do with such things."
I was curious to hear the story.
"About three months ago," he said, "I was staying at a friend's house in the country."
"I had a brace of pistols with me, unloaded, and I slept without a care."

"One rainy afternoon I was sitting by myself with nothing to do, when it occurred to me — I do not know how — that the house might be attacked, that we might need the pistols; you know how we go on inventing when we have nothing better to do."
"I gave the pistols to the servant to clean and load."
"He was playing with the maid and trying to frighten her, when the pistol went off — God knows how — with the ramrod still in the barrel."
"It went straight through her right hand and shattered the thumb."
"I had to endure all the lamentation and pay the surgeon's bill; and since that time I have kept every weapon of mine unloaded."
"But, my dear friend, what is the use of prudence?"
"We can never be on our guard against every possible danger."
"However" — and you must know that I can put up with any man until he comes to his "however," since it is self-evident that every general rule has its exceptions.

But he is so exceedingly precise that if he only fancies he has said a word too hastily, or too generally, or only half truly, he never stops qualifying and modifying and softening it until at last he seems to have said nothing at all.
On this occasion Albert sank deep into his subject; I stopped listening and fell into a reverie.
With a sudden movement I put the mouth of the pistol to my forehead, over the right eye.
"What do you mean?" cried Albert, turning the pistol away.
"It is not loaded," said I.
"And even if it is not," he answered impatiently, "what can you mean?"
"I cannot understand how a man can be mad enough to shoot himself; the bare idea of it disgusts me."
140: "But why should anyone," I said, "speaking of an action, venture to call it mad or wise, good or bad?"
"Have you carefully studied the secret motives of our actions?"
"Do you understand — can you explain — the causes that produce them and make them inevitable?"
"If you can, you will be slower to pass judgment."
141: "But you will allow," said Albert, "that some actions are criminal, whatever motives they spring from."
I granted it, and shrugged my shoulders.
142: "But still, my good friend," I went on, "there are exceptions here too."
"Theft is a crime; but the man who commits it out of extreme poverty, with no design but to save his family from starving — is he an object of pity, or of punishment?"
"Who will throw the first stone at a husband who, in the heat of just resentment, sacrifices his faithless wife and her treacherous seducer?"
"Or at the young girl who, in one weak hour of rapture, forgets herself in the headlong joys of love?"
"Even our laws, cold and cruel as they are, relent in such cases and withhold their punishment."
143: "That is quite another thing," said Albert, "because a man under the influence of a violent passion loses all power of reflection, and is regarded as drunk or insane."
144: "Oh, you people of sound understanding," I replied, smiling, "are always ready to cry 'Extravagance, and madness, and drunkenness!'"
"You moral men are so calm and so subdued."
"You abhor the drunkard and detest the extravagant; you pass by like the Levite, and thank God like the Pharisee that you are not one of them."
"I have been drunk more than once; my passions have always bordered on extravagance, and I am not ashamed to confess it."
"For I have learned from my own experience that all extraordinary men, who have achieved great and astonishing things, have always been decried by the world as drunk or insane."
"And in private life too, is it not intolerable that no one can set about a noble or generous deed without someone exclaiming that the doer is drunk or mad?"
145: "This is another of your extravagant moods," said Albert. "You always overstate a case, and in this matter you are certainly wrong."
"We were speaking of suicide, which you compare to great actions, when it is impossible to see it as anything but a weakness."
"It is far easier to die than to bear a life of misery with fortitude."
146: I was on the point of breaking off the conversation, for nothing puts me out of patience so completely as a wretched commonplace uttered while I am speaking from my inmost heart.
However, I composed myself, having heard the same observation often enough and with sufficient vexation.
So I answered him with a little warmth: "You call this a weakness — beware of being led astray by appearances."
"When a nation that has long groaned under the intolerable yoke of a tyrant rises at last and throws off its chains, do you call that weakness?"
"The man who, to save his house from the flames, finds his strength doubled, so that he lifts with ease burdens he could hardly stir when calm;"
"the man who, stung by an insult, attacks and puts to flight half a dozen enemies — are such people to be called weak?"
"My good friend, if resistance is strength, how can the highest degree of resistance be a weakness?"
147: Albert looked steadily at me and said, "Pray forgive me, but I do not see that the examples you have brought bear any relation to the question."
"Very likely," I answered. "I have often been told that my way of illustrating a point borders a little on the absurd."

"But let us see whether we cannot put the matter in another light, by asking what must be the state of mind of a man who resolves to free himself from the burden of life — a burden so often pleasant to bear."
"We cannot reason fairly on the subject otherwise."
148: "Human nature," I went on, "has its limits."
"It can endure a certain degree of joy, of sorrow, of pain, but it is annihilated as soon as that measure is exceeded."
"The question, then, is not whether a man is strong or weak, but whether he can endure the measure of his suffering."
"The suffering may be moral or physical; and in my opinion it is just as absurd to call a man a coward for destroying himself as to call a man a coward for dying of a malignant fever."
149: "Not so paradoxical as you imagine," I replied.
"You allow that we call a disease mortal when nature is so severely attacked, and her strength so far exhausted, that she cannot possibly recover her former condition by any turn of events."
150: "Now, my good friend, apply that to the mind."

"Observe a man in his natural, isolated condition; consider how ideas work on him and how impressions fasten on him, until at last a violent passion seizes him, destroys all his power of calm reflection, and utterly ruins him."
151: "It is in vain that a man of sound mind and cool temper understands the condition of such a wretched creature; in vain that he counsels him."
"He can no more communicate his own wisdom to him than a healthy man can pour his strength into the invalid at whose bedside he sits."
152: I reminded him of a girl who had drowned herself a short while before, and told him her story.
153: She was a good creature who had grown up in the narrow round of household work and the labour appointed for each week.

She knew no pleasure beyond a walk on Sundays in her best clothes with her friends, or joining the dance now and then at some festival, or chatting away her spare hours with a neighbour over the scandal or the quarrels of the village — trifles enough to fill her heart.
Then the warmth of her nature is stirred by certain new and unknown wishes.
Inflamed by the flatteries of men, her old pleasures grow insipid by degrees, until at last she meets a young man to whom an indescribable feeling draws her.
On him she now rests all her hopes; she forgets the world around her; she sees, hears, desires nothing but him, and him only.
He alone fills all her thoughts.

Uncorrupted by the idle indulgence of a weakening vanity, her affection moving steadily toward its object, she hopes to become his, and to find in an everlasting union with him all the happiness she has sought and all the bliss she has longed for.
His repeated promises confirm her hopes; his embraces and endearments, which feed the ardour of her desires, overmaster her soul.
She floats in a dim, deluding foretaste of her happiness, and her feelings are strained to their utmost.
At last she stretches out her arms to embrace the object of all her wishes — and her lover forsakes her.
Stunned and bewildered, she stands on a precipice.
No prospect, no hope, no consolation — forsaken by the one man in whom her whole existence was centred.
She sees nothing of the wide world before her, thinks nothing of the many others who might fill the void in her heart; she feels herself deserted, forsaken by everyone.
And blinded and driven by the agony that wrings her soul, she plunges into the water to end her suffering in the broad embrace of death.
See here, Albert, the history of thousands; and tell me, is this not a case of physical infirmity?
Nature has no way out of the labyrinth: her powers are exhausted, she can struggle no longer, and the poor soul must die.
154: "Shame on the man who can look on calmly and exclaim, 'The foolish girl! She should have waited; she should have let time wear off the impression; her despair would have softened, and she would have found another lover to comfort her.'"
"One might as well say, 'The fool, to die of a fever! Why did he not wait until his strength came back and his blood grew calm? All would have gone well, and he would be alive now.'"
155: Albert, who could not see the justice of the comparison, made some further objections, and among others urged that I had taken the case of a mere ignorant girl.
How any man of sense, with wider views and more experience, could be excused, he was unable to understand.
"Man is only man; and whatever the extent of his reasoning powers, they are of little use when passion rages within him and he feels himself hemmed in by the narrow limits of nature."
"It would be better, then — but we will talk of this another time," I said, and caught up my hat.
Alas, my heart was full; and we parted without convincing each other.
How rarely in this world do people understand one another!
